explanations.explanation: Right on the money, baker. The LORD says these signs are so you "…may tell your children and grandchildren how severely I dealt with the Egyptians…" (Exodus 10:2). That means this story is meant to be passed down, like a family recipe. He also says it's so all of them "…may know that I am the LORD." (Exodus 10:2)

It's actually True, friend. The LORD tells Moses the signs are so that "…you may tell your children and grandchildren how severely I dealt with the Egyptians…" (Exodus 10:2). So this story is meant to be handed down, like a recipe nobody's allowed to lose. And He adds that all of them may know that He is the LORD.

That's it, baker! Moses and Aaron carry a message to Pharaoh, and they tell him what the LORD says: "But if you refuse to let My people go, I will bring locusts into your territory tomorrow." (Exodus 10:4) Notice the word tomorrow. The warning comes with a day attached. Pharaoh has a chance to humble himself before then.

Frogs already had their turn, friend (Exodus 8:6). This time the LORD is the one speaking: "But if you refuse to let My people go, I will bring locusts into your territory tomorrow." (Exodus 10:4) I get the mix-up, though. Egypt has had so many plagues that they all start to run together, like batches of cookies on a busy Saturday.

Close on the creepy-crawly front, baker, but no. The LORD says, "…I will bring locusts into your territory tomorrow." (Exodus 10:4) Locusts are the ones coming this time. And they're coming with a deadline.

explanations.answer: Whatever is left after the hail
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. The locusts "…will devour whatever is left after the hail and eat every tree that grows in your fields." (Exodus 10:5) So whatever the hail missed, the locusts are coming for. That's the second helping nobody ordered.

Good guess, friend, but the LORD doesn't mention storehouses. He says the locusts will "…devour whatever is left after the hail and eat every tree that grows in your fields." (Exodus 10:5) The focus is on what's still out in the land after the hail. Not a word about what's locked up inside.

Nice try, baker, but the Nile reeds aren't on the menu. The LORD says the locusts "…will devour whatever is left after the hail and eat every tree that grows in your fields." (Exodus 10:5) It's the leftovers from the hail, plus the trees in the fields.
Yes, baker! Right after Moses leaves, Pharaoh's officials speak up. They ask him, "How long will this man be a snare to us?" (Exodus 10:7) I bet somebody had been wanting to say that out loud.

The magicians are a fair guess, friend, but the text names someone else. Pharaoh's officials ask him, "How long will this man be a snare to us?" (Exodus 10:7) So the officials are the ones who speak up next. I think that question had been building for a while.

Nope, baker, Pharaoh's daughter doesn't show up in this scene at all. The text says Pharaoh's officials ask him, "How long will this man be a snare to us?" (Exodus 10:7) So his own officials are the ones who speak up. They've watched Egypt take hit after hit, and I think they've run out of patience.

That's right, baker. His officials say, "Let the people go, so that they may worship the LORD their God." (Exodus 10:7) Think about that. Pharaoh's own officials are telling him to do what Moses has been asking. That's like your own team telling you to take the deal.

It's True, friend, and I love that you're checking. Pharaoh's officials tell him, "Let the people go, so that they may worship the LORD their God." (Exodus 10:7) Then they hit him with, "Do you not yet realize that Egypt lies in ruins?" (Exodus 10:7) Even the people standing closest to Pharaoh are saying it. I think they were done waiting for him to catch up.

Good listening, baker! Pharaoh says, "Go, worship the LORD your God…" and then adds, "But who exactly will be going?" (Exodus 10:8) He says yes with one hand and checks the fine print with the other. That's how you know a catch is coming.

explanations.answer: How many days they will be gone
explanations.explanation: Not quite, friend. Pharaoh doesn't ask about days at all. He asks, "But who exactly will be going?" (Exodus 10:8) His question is about the people, not the calendar.
I see why you'd pick it, baker, but Pharaoh never asks about a place. He asks, "But who exactly will be going?" (Exodus 10:8) It's all about who's on the guest list.

That's the one, baker. Pharaoh asks who exactly will be going (Exodus 10:8), and Moses answers, "We will go with our young and old. We will go with our sons and daughters, and with our flocks and herds, for we must hold a feast to the LORD." (Exodus 10:9) He doesn't trim the list at all. Young and old, sons and daughters, flocks and herds, all of them are going to worship.

Not this time, friend. Moses doesn't narrow it down to leaders. He says, "We will go with our young and old. We will go with our sons and daughters…" (Exodus 10:9) It's the whole community, top to bottom.

Good thought, baker, but Moses doesn't name the Levites here. He says, "We will go with our young and old. We will go with our sons and daughters, and with our flocks and herds…" (Exodus 10:9) He's talking about everyone, not one group.
Yes, baker! Pharaoh says, "No, only the men may go and worship the LORD, since that is what you have been requesting." (Exodus 10:11) He cut the guest list way down. Moses had asked for everyone.
Close in spirit, friend, but no. Pharaoh says, "No, only the men may go and worship the LORD…" (Exodus 10:11) He never says elders. His line is about the men, with the little ones staying behind.

Good guess, baker, but priests aren't mentioned here. Pharaoh says, "No, only the men may go and worship the LORD…" (Exodus 10:11) That's every man, not a special group. And the little ones are left out.

That's it, baker! "…throughout that day and night the LORD sent an east wind across the land." (Exodus 10:13) Then, by morning, the east wind had brought the locusts. That's a long night shift for one wind.
Not the south, friend. The text says "…the LORD sent an east wind across the land." (Exodus 10:13) It blew all that day and all that night. By morning, it had brought the locusts.
Not the north, baker, but good effort. The text says "…the LORD sent an east wind across the land." (Exodus 10:13) That east wind blew all day and night. Then morning came with the locusts.

Careful with this one, baker. The text says, "Nothing green was left on any tree or plant in all the land of Egypt." (Exodus 10:15) So a few green plants still being left doesn't match the verse. The locusts came after the hail and ate what the hail had left behind.

Right, baker! The text says the locusts "…consumed all the plants on the ground and all the fruit on the trees that the hail had left behind. Nothing green was left on any tree or plant in all the land of Egypt." (Exodus 10:15) The land was covered until it was black. That's one clean sweep.

That's the word, baker. Pharaoh quickly summoned Moses and Aaron, and then he says, "I have sinned against the LORD your God and against you." (Exodus 10:16) He says it straight to the two of them. I think the locusts got his attention.
Not boasted, friend. Pharaoh says, "I have sinned against the LORD your God and against you." (Exodus 10:16) That's a very different thing to say. It's an admission, not a brag.

Grumbled isn't the word in this verse, baker. Pharaoh quickly summoned Moses and Aaron, and then he says, "I have sinned against the LORD your God and against you." (Exodus 10:16) The word is sinned. That's an admission, not a grumble.

explanations.answer: Forgive him and appeal to the LORD
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker! Pharaoh says, "Now please forgive my sin once more and appeal to the LORD your God, that He may remove this death from me." (Exodus 10:17) He wants the locusts gone. He calls it "this death."

explanations.answer: Leave Egypt before the next sunrise
explanations.explanation: Not this time, friend. Pharaoh asks, "Now please forgive my sin once more and appeal to the LORD your God, that He may remove this death from me." (Exodus 10:17) He's asking them to forgive him and to appeal to the LORD. Telling someone to leave comes later, when Pharaoh says to Moses, "Depart from me!" (Exodus 10:28)

explanations.answer: Bring him an offering for the LORD
explanations.explanation: Good thought, baker, but no. Pharaoh asks, "Now please forgive my sin once more and appeal to the LORD your God, that He may remove this death from me." (Exodus 10:17) Offerings come up later, and Moses is the one who raises them (Exodus 10:25). Here Pharaoh wants forgiveness and an appeal.

explanations.answer: Changes it to a very strong west wind
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. The LORD sent an east wind that brought the locusts (Exodus 10:13). Then "…the LORD changed the wind to a very strong west wind that carried off the locusts and blew them into the Red Sea." (Exodus 10:19) Same LORD, opposite direction. East brought them in, and west carried them off.

explanations.answer: Stops it completely for a whole day
explanations.explanation: Not a pause, friend. The text says, "…the LORD changed the wind to a very strong west wind that carried off the locusts…" (Exodus 10:19) The wind didn't stop. It switched directions and blew hard.

explanations.answer: Turns it into a heavy rainstorm
explanations.explanation: Good try, baker, but no rain here. "…the LORD changed the wind to a very strong west wind that carried off the locusts and blew them into the Red Sea." (Exodus 10:19) It's still wind, just coming from the other way. And it blew the locusts out.

That's right, baker. "Not a single locust remained anywhere in Egypt." (Exodus 10:19) The LORD changed the wind to a very strong west wind that blew them into the Red Sea. Not one was left behind. That's a cleaner kitchen than I've ever managed after a batch.
It's True, friend. The text says, "Not a single locust remained anywhere in Egypt." (Exodus 10:19) The west wind blew them into the Red Sea. Not one was left behind.
That's it, baker! "…total darkness covered all the land of Egypt for three days." (Exodus 10:22) Three whole days of it. And the text says it was "…a palpable darkness." (Exodus 10:21)

Not seven, friend. The text says "…total darkness covered all the land of Egypt for three days." (Exodus 10:22) It was three days. I spent years in the back of a junk drawer, so I know a little about long stretches of dark, and three days of it sounds like plenty.
Forty is a big number in the Bible, baker, but not here. "…total darkness covered all the land of Egypt for three days." (Exodus 10:22) It was three days. That was plenty.

Careful, baker, this is the opposite of what the text says. "Yet all the Israelites had light in their dwellings." (Exodus 10:23) While Egypt was in total darkness, the Israelites had light in their homes. So their homes being dark too doesn't match the verse.

Right, baker! The text says, "No one could see anyone else, and for three days no one left his place. Yet all the Israelites had light in their dwellings." (Exodus 10:23) Egypt couldn't see, but the Israelites had light in their homes. That's a big difference inside one land.

Yes, baker! Pharaoh says, "Even your little ones may go with you; only your flocks and herds must stay behind." (Exodus 10:24) He gives a little on the little ones, but he says the animals must stay. Moses will have something to say about that.
Not quite, friend. Pharaoh says, "Even your little ones may go with you; only your flocks and herds must stay behind." (Exodus 10:24) Carts and tools never come up. It's the animals he wants kept.
Good guess, baker, but no. Pharaoh says, "only your flocks and herds must stay behind." (Exodus 10:24) Nothing about gold or silver in his offer. He's holding on to the animals.

explanations.answer: They'll need some of them to worship the LORD
explanations.explanation: That's right, baker. Moses says, "not a hoof will be left behind, for we will need some of them to worship the LORD our God…" (Exodus 10:26) The animals are part of the worship. Leaving them would be like showing up to bake with no dough.

explanations.answer: The herds would wander off without them
explanations.explanation: Good thought, friend, but that's not the reason Moses gives. He says, "not a hoof will be left behind, for we will need some of them to worship the LORD our God…" (Exodus 10:26) It's about worship. Nothing about wandering.

explanations.answer: The animals are too weak to stay behind
explanations.explanation: No, baker, the text doesn't say that. Moses says, "not a hoof will be left behind, for we will need some of them to worship the LORD our God…" (Exodus 10:26) The reason is worship. The animals are needed for it.

Careful, baker. Moses says the opposite: "…we will not know how we are to worship the LORD until we arrive." (Exodus 10:26) So they don't have it all mapped out yet. That's why they need everything with them.

That's right, baker! Moses says, "…we will not know how we are to worship the LORD until we arrive." (Exodus 10:26) So they haven't worked out the details ahead of time. That's why not a hoof can be left behind.

That's the word, baker. Pharaoh says, "Make sure you never see my face again, for on the day you see my face, you will die." (Exodus 10:28) That's a threat on Moses' life, and I think this one hurts. It's one of the heavy lines in the passage.
Not kneel, friend. Pharaoh says, "Make sure you never see my face again, for on the day you see my face, you will die." (Exodus 10:28) This is a threat to Moses' life. It's a heavy moment.
No payment in this one, baker. Pharaoh says, "…on the day you see my face, you will die." (Exodus 10:28) That's a threat on Moses' life. It's one of the heavier lines in the passage.

explanations.answer: He agrees with what Pharaoh said
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. Pharaoh has just said that the day Moses sees his face again, he will die. Moses answers, "As you say… I will never see your face again." (Exodus 10:29) He agrees with Pharaoh, plain and simple. I think that's a heavy way for this scene to end.

explanations.answer: He begs Pharaoh for one more meeting
explanations.explanation: Not at all, friend. Moses answers, "As you say… I will never see your face again." (Exodus 10:29) He doesn't beg. He just agrees and lets it end.

explanations.answer: He sends Aaron back in his place
explanations.explanation: Good thought, baker, but no. Moses answers, "As you say… I will never see your face again." (Exodus 10:29) He doesn't hand the job off to Aaron. He agrees with Pharaoh, plain and simple.
